chunks: "Oversampling means the receiver samples the incoming line much faster than the bit rate, typically 16 times per bit.
It uses an internal clock at 16 times the baud rate and counts ticks. How it's implemented: the receiver watches the line on every tick.
When it sees a falling edge, that's the start bit, and it starts counting. Eight ticks later it's in the middle of the start bit, and it checks it's still low to reject glitches.
After that it samples once every 16 ticks, so each sample lands in the middle of a bit.
Many UARTs also take three samples, around ticks 7, 8 and 9, and do a majority vote, so a single noisy sample doesn't flip the bit.
Why it's needed: there's no clock, so the receiver has to find the bit boundaries from one edge.
If it only sampled once per bit time, it wouldn't know where the edge was to within a whole bit, and it couldn't centre itself or reject noise.
With 16 samples per bit it knows the edge to within one sixteenth of a bit.
Common rates are 16x, which is the classic standard, and 8x, which many modern MCUs offer as an option so they can reach higher baud rates from the same clock.
Some chips also use other factors, but 16 and 8 are the ones to know."
